A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MTR-Bench, with the same four categories, 40 tasks, and 3,600 instances. Their text, equations, figures, and tables are readable. v1 ends with references; v3 adds Appendices A–N, which were included in the comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 20 models, including accuracy, interaction-turn efficiency, invalid operations, and reasoning-pattern results.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds Qwen3 evaluations, supplementary efficiency and stability results, failure analysis, and a preliminary reinforcement-learning experiment.

M1.justification: The Generator–Monitor–Evaluator framework and core evaluation procedure are retained. Appendix N.2 adds a limited training adaptation: using MTR-Bench environmental feedback as the reinforcement-learning reward for R1-1.5B. The extensive pseudocode elsewhere primarily documents existing components.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same four-category, 40-task benchmark with 3,600 instances. Appendix L documents the existing tasks rather than establishing additional coverage. The supplementary analyses and RL experiment use MTR-Bench; no additional evaluated dataset or domain is identified.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains all 20 original models and adds five Qwen3 configurations: 235B-A22B, 32B, 8B, and 1.7B Thinking models, plus Qwen3-8B-IT. This extends the comparison within one model family. Appendix I provides source-problem difficulty ratings, not an experimentally evaluated human comparator.

E3.justification: v3 adds supplementary evaluation procedures, including average-turn and token-consumption comparisons, inspection of 50 sampled failures, and an RL before-and-after evaluation. The main instance count, difficulty levels, and 15-turn cap remain unchanged. Appendix F's inference and aggregation settings are newly disclosed, without establishing changes to the original experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained turn, efficiency, invalid-operation, and reasoning-pattern analyses, v3 adds an R1 pass@16 stability check, computational-efficiency analysis, and a five-category failure taxonomy based on 50 sampled failures. Appendix N also tests the benchmark's utility for RL training. These substantially broaden the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without uncertainty reporting. v3 adds 95% confidence intervals for the original 20-model comparison in Table 7 and standard deviations from supplementary R1 pass@16 experiments in Table 4. Interval construction and random seeds are unspecified; the additions do not establish that all main experiments were rerun.

E6.justification: All original Table 1 model values are retained, but five Qwen3 result rows are added; Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking leads medium/hard Dynamic Adaptation with 25.80/20.30. Tables 5–6 add turn-count and token-consumption results. Appendix N newly reports R1-1.5B accuracy increasing from 6.25% to 22.27% after RL, with insufficient setting details to compare those values directly against v1's table.

T1.justification: Appendix A adds an explicit mathematical formulation of query generation from the problem and interaction history, q_i = f_theta(p, H_{i-1}). Appendix C adds a simple one-turn guessing-probability argument. The original framework and metric equations remain unchanged, and no substantial theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contributions: a diverse multi-turn reasoning benchmark, automated evaluation with adjustable difficulty, and evidence of current models' weaknesses. The added appendix applications and analyses do not materially redefine these main claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning structured interaction formats, natural-language dialogue coverage, random opponents, and the 15-turn cap's disadvantage for slower-solving models. Appendices C, E, K, and N expand explanations of multi-turn requirements, failure mechanisms, and training implications. Appendix I additionally interprets Codeforces ratings as a proxy for human difficulty.

D1.justification: v3 supplies all 40 task templates and difficulty settings, framework and task pseudocode, source counts of 32 Codeforces and eight New York Times tasks, and a code/data access link. Appendix F adds inference settings, including R1 temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.95, plus H800 hardware and computational-cost information. These substantially expand documentation rather than establish wholesale implementation changes.

R1.justification: Appendix B and Table 3 substantially expand positioning across static evaluation, real-world agents, formal planning, and interactive games. New comparisons discuss AgentBench, AgentBoard, TRAC, ACPBench, ActionReasoningBench, and SPIN-Bench, emphasizing abstract reasoning and parametric generation. The earlier MINT discussion and several game-related references are removed.

P1.justification: v3 extensively expands procedural explanations and task-by-task exposition through Appendices A–N. It also condenses and rewrites Sections 4.4–4.6 and the main related-work section, and adds dedicated Limitations and Ethics sections. Authorship details and citation style also change.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column to a two-column layout, with retained figures relocated or resized. Table 1 gains model rows, and Tables 3–7 add benchmark comparisons, supplementary results, and an uncertainty-enhanced redisplay of original accuracy results. Numerous boxed task descriptions and 16 algorithm displays substantially expand the visual organization.

improvement.justification: v3 makes the benchmark easier to inspect through task templates, implementation descriptions, experimental settings, access information, and explicit limitations missing from v1. However, new inconsistencies limit the gain: Algorithm 3 reverses the impostor-feedback labels retained in Section 3.3, confidence-interval construction is unexplained, and the RL experiment lacks reproducible training and evaluation details. The added transparency supports a positive but qualified overall improvement.
